## Cross Product
Take the cross of two vectors to find the one perpendicular to both.

I know this sounds useless in 2D, but trust me it's still handy!

$$\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
A_yB_z - A_zB_y\\
A_zB_x - A_xB_z \\
A_xB_y - A_yB_x
\end{pmatrix}$$

. . . 

I actually memorize that by taking the determinant of this matrix (where $i, j, k$ point along $x, y, z$)

$$\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \text{det}\begin{pmatrix}
i & j & k\\
A_x & A_y & A_z\\
B_x & B_y & B_z 
\end{pmatrix}$$

## Dot Product

Take the dot product between two vectors to find out something about the angle between them. 

$$\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = \|\vec{A}\|\|\vec{B}\|\cos \theta$$

where $\|\vec{A}\|$ and $\|\vec{B}\|$ are the magnitude of the two vectors and $\theta$ is the angle between them.

. . .

Amazingly, the formula above is the same as:

$$\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = A_xB_x + A_yB_y$$

. . .

Dot product is also great to figure out the length of one vector "along" another vector:

$$\text{Length of }\vec{A} \text{ along } \vec{B} = \vec{A} \cdot \hat{B}$$

where $\hat{B}$ is the normalized version of $\vec{B}$. Point along that length by multiplying by vector's direction:

$$\vec{A} \text{ projected onto } \vec{B} = (\vec{A} \cdot \hat{B})\hat{B}$$
